title: Why does `LIMIT ... OFFSET` pagination get slower on deep pages (the DB scans and discards all preceding rows: O(n) per page), and how does keyset/cursor pagination (`WHERE id > :last_seen ORDER BY id LIMIT n`) stay O(log n) at any depth?
shortTitle: Why LIMIT/OFFSET pagination gets slower on deep pages, and keyset pagination

s1_definition.oneliner: OFFSET re-reads everything before the page (slower the deeper you go); keyset seeks straight to the page using the last-seen key (fast at any depth).
s1_definition.profdef:
- **OFFSET cost** – `LIMIT n OFFSET m` forces the database to read and discard all `m` preceding rows before returning the page, so cost grows as O(m).
- **Keyset pagination** – `WHERE id > :last_seen ORDER BY id LIMIT n` uses an index seek to jump directly to the start of the page, so cost is O(log n) at any depth.
- **Stability** – OFFSET shifts under concurrent inserts (duplicates or skips); keyset is anchored to a real key.
- **Trade-off** – keyset gives next/previous navigation, not arbitrary jump-to-page-N.
- **Composite cursor** – for multi-column ordering, use a row-value comparison like `(created_at, id) > (:last_ts, :last_id)`.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh wants page five hundred of his transaction history at National Bank of India. With OFFSET, the clerk counts past ten thousand transactions one by one and throws them away just to hand over the next ten. With keyset, Rajesh says "continue from the last transaction I saw," and the clerk uses the index to jump straight there: just as fast on page five hundred as on page one.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  OFFSET pagination:                   Keyset pagination:

  SELECT ... LIMIT 10 OFFSET 9990     SELECT ... WHERE id > 110 LIMIT 10

  ┌──────────────────────┐             ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ Read row 1           │             │ B-tree seek to 110   │
  │ Read row 2           │             │ Read row 111         │
  │ ...                  │             │ Read row 112         │
  │ Read row 9990        │             │ ...                  │
  │ (all discarded!)     │             │ Read row 120         │
  │ Return rows 9991-10000│            │ Return rows 111-120  │
  └──────────────────────┘             └──────────────────────┘

  Cost: O(9990)                        Cost: O(log n + 10)
  Slow on deep pages                   Same speed at any depth
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Offset pagination gets slower on deep pages because the database cannot skip ahead. For LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10000, it must read and discard all ten thousand preceding rows before returning the next ten. That waste grows linearly with the offset, so page one is instant but page one thousand crawls.

Keyset pagination fixes this by replacing the offset with a WHERE condition on the last-seen key. Instead of skipping rows, the database performs a B-tree seek directly to the cursor and reads only the page. The cost is O(log n) at any depth, identical whether on page one or page one million.

The cursor must be on a unique, ordered column or a unique composite, backed by a matching index. The trade-off is that keyset gives next/previous navigation rather than arbitrary jump-to-page-N, which is exactly right for transaction histories, feeds, and APIs. Keyset also handles concurrent inserts correctly because it is anchored to a real key rather than a row count.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh's multi-year transaction history loaded instantly on the first pages but stalled for seconds once he scrolled deep. Replacing offset with keyset pagination anchored on the transaction id pair made deep pages as fast as the first page.

Remember one sentence: OFFSET re-reads everything before the page while keyset seeks straight to it, so keyset stays fast at any depth.

---

keyPoints: OFFSET forces the database to read and discard all preceding rows, so cost grows linearly with page depth.
Keyset pagination uses WHERE id > :last_seen with an index seek, so cost is O(log n) at any depth.
Offset pagination causes duplicates and skips under concurrent inserts; keyset is stable.
The cursor must be on a unique, ordered column or a unique composite backed by a matching index.
For multi-column ordering, use a composite cursor like (created_at, id) > (:last_ts, :last_id).
Keyset gives next/previous navigation, not arbitrary jump-to-page-N, which suits APIs and feeds.
Consider encoding the cursor as an opaque base64 token to prevent client tampering.
